title: Find the Lexicographically Largest String From the Box I
statement:
You are given a string `word` and an integer `numFriends`. A *split* cuts `word` into exactly `numFriends` non-empty consecutive pieces that, read in order, spell `word`. Go through every different split of `word` and gather all of their pieces in one collection. Return the lexicographically largest string in that collection.

Strings compare letter by letter: at the first position where they differ, the one with the later letter is larger, and when one string is a prefix of the other, the longer string is larger.
constraints: word consists only of lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every split is exponential, which is what the brute force does on tiny words. Instead, ask which pieces can appear at all. With a single friend nothing is cut, so the only piece is the whole word. Otherwise a piece that starts at index `i` must leave `numFriends - 1` other non-empty pieces, so it has at most `n - numFriends + 1` characters, or fewer if the word ends first. That longest piece always occurs in some split, because the characters left over can be cut into the other `numFriends - 1` pieces. Among the pieces that start at `i` it is also the largest, since a string beats each of its own prefixes. So there is one candidate per start: enumerate the starts and keep the largest.

## Approach

1. If `numFriends === 1`, the only piece is `word` itself: return it.
2. Otherwise a piece has at most `longest = word.length - numFriends + 1` characters.
3. For each start `i`, take `candidate = word.substring(i, i + longest)`, which is shorter near the end of the word.
4. Keep the lexicographically largest `candidate` in `best` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`word = "dbca"` and `numFriends = 2`, so `longest = 3`. The candidates are `"dbc"` (`i = 0`), `"bca"` (`i = 1`), `"ca"` (`i = 2`) and `"a"` (`i = 3`). Only `"dbc"` starts with the largest letter, `d`, so `best = "dbc"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · (n − numFriends + 1)): n candidates, each built and compared in up to `longest` steps.
- Space: O(n) for the current candidate and `best`.

## Pitfalls

- One friend is special: the whole word is the only piece, even when a suffix such as `"c"` in `"abc"` would compare larger.
- The first occurrence of the largest letter is not always best: `"zazb"` with 2 friends gives `"zb"`, which beats `"zaz"`.
- A longer string beats its own prefix, so take the longest piece from each start, not a shorter one.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `longest` | the most characters one piece can have |
| `i` | the start of the current candidate |
| `candidate` | the longest piece that starts at `i` |
| `best` | the largest candidate so far |

narration.2: With one friend the word is never cut...
narration.3: ...so the whole word is the only piece in the collection.
narration.5: The other numFriends - 1 pieces need at least one letter each, which caps the length of any piece.
narration.6: The empty string is smaller than every candidate, so it is a safe start.
narration.7: Try every index as the start of a piece.
narration.8: The longest piece from this start is the largest one starting here; substring stops at the end of the word.
narration.9: Is this candidate lexicographically larger than the best so far?
narration.13: Return the largest piece any split can produce.
